Cl C Cl C H Cl Growth Hormone and its Modulators 1798 Human growth is under a complex system of hormonal controls. Growth hormone is produced by specialised cells (somatotropes) in the anterior pituitary; produc- tion and secretion are under a system of double regula- tion by a release-inhibiting hormone, somatostatin, and a growth hormone-releasing hormone, somatorelin, both produced in the hypothalamus. These in turn are modulated by various stimuli: dopamine, serotonin, hypoglycaemia, stress or emotional excitement, and ingestion of protein-rich meals all stimulate growth hormone release, whereas glucose, free fatty acids, in- sulin-like growth factor and growth hormone itself all suppress it. The effects of growth hormone in the body rely on its interaction with a distinct growth hormone receptor; some effects, such as stimulation of lipolysis and glu- coneogenesis, are direct but others, including its ana- bolic and growth-promoting effects, are mediated by induction of insulin-like growth factors (somatomed- ins). Included in this chapter are growth hormone itself, now generally given as recombinant somatropin (p.1799) or its synthetic methionyl analogue somatrem (p.1799), and somatomedins such as mecasermin (p.1807). Also included are the hypothalamic releasing hormone, somatorelin (p.1808), and its analogue ser- morelin (p.1808); the hypothalamic inhibiting hor- mone, somatostatin (p.1809), and its analogues such as lanreotide (p.1803) and octreotide (p.1803); the growth hormone release stimulant pralmorelin (p.1807); and the growth hormone-receptor antagonist pegvisomant (p.1807).
